creative.body:
I was doubled over in the passenger seat begging my husband to drive faster. I thought my intestine had ruptured.

The pain started at 6 AM. Right side, just below my ribs. Sharp enough that I couldn't stand up straight. By 8, I was sweating through my shirt and my husband was grabbing the keys without asking.

Twenty-seven pounds. That's what I'd lost on Mounjaro in five months. Twenty-seven pounds that made my doctor smile at my checkup. That got my sister-in-law to pull me aside at Easter and whisper "what are you doing, because whatever it is, I need it."

Twenty-seven pounds that were costing me everything below my throat.

The constipation started around week three. My prescriber said it was normal. The internet said it was normal. Drink more water. Eat more fiber. Give your body time to adjust.

I did all of it. My body never adjusted.

By month two, I was going once every five or six days. Forty-five minutes on the toilet producing almost nothing. Sweating. Pushing until I saw stars. Leaving the bathroom feeling like I hadn't gone at all.

I stopped wearing anything with a waistband. My stomach was so distended my daughter asked if I was pregnant. I'm forty-four. I'd just lost twenty-seven pounds. And my twelve-year-old was asking if there was a baby.

That's the sentence. That's what nobody posts in the before-and-after photos. You lose the weight and your gut goes to prison.

I was taking Miralax every single day. Sometimes twice. Dulcolax in my purse, my car, my nightstand. Smooth Move tea from Amazon. Magnesium citrate. Psyllium husk. Prune juice that made me gag.

None of it mattered. Everything either did nothing or made me so bloated I looked six months along. The sulfur burps started around month three — hot, rotten-egg belches that came without warning. I was in a meeting with my regional director when one came up mid-sentence. I pretended to cough. She pretended not to notice. I spent the rest of the day wanting to disappear.

That's what the sentence looks like. Not just the bathroom. The meetings you dread. The dinners you skip. The mornings you wonder how a medication that's supposed to make your body smaller has made your stomach bigger.

Then came the morning I thought it was my appendix.

The ER moved fast once I said the pain was an eight. CT scan. Blood draw. IV for fluids.

When the doctor came in with the results, I was expecting something serious. Obstruction. Rupture. Something that matched the pain.

"Severe fecal loading," he said. "Your colon is completely backed up. No obstruction. No rupture."

He said it flatly. Like he was reading a weather report.

My husband was sitting in the chair by the window. I couldn't look at him. I'd dragged him to the emergency room at 8 AM on a Saturday and the CT scan showed I was full of stool. I was so constipated my body thought it was dying, and the hospital told me I just needed to poop.

That shame — I wouldn't wish it on anyone.

But then he said something during discharge that I almost missed.

He was scanning my medication list. Mounjaro. The dosage. How long I'd been on it. He looked up from the chart and said, "Everything you've been taking treats below the dam. Your problem is the dam itself."

He didn't explain. He had another patient waiting. He handed me the discharge papers and walked out.

I sat in the car for ten minutes before my husband started the engine. He thought I was upset about the diagnosis. I was. But I was also turning that sentence over in my head.

Below the dam. The dam itself.

The Mounjaro. It slows your stomach down — that's the whole point. That's how it kills your appetite. Your stomach holds food longer, so you feel full faster.

But mine hadn't just slowed down. It had stopped. Food was sitting in my stomach so long it was fermenting — that's where the sulfur burps came from, the bloating, all of it. And because nothing was moving through my stomach, nothing was reaching my intestines. My entire digestive system downstream had dried up.

Every single thing I'd been taking — Miralax, Dulcolax, magnesium, the fiber — was trying to get things moving at the bottom. But nothing was reaching the bottom in the first place.

I'd been pouring water at the bottom of a dry riverbed for five months. The river wasn't flowing because something was blocking it at the top. And I never once thought to look upstream.

I couldn't sleep that night. I lay in bed turning that ER doctor's ten words over in my head, feeling like an idiot for every Miralax dose I'd ever measured.

The next morning I started researching. Not Googling "constipation remedies" like I'd done a hundred times. This time I searched for what helps a stomach actually move food through when a medication has slowed it down.

Completely different results.

Most of what came up was useless — the same fiber recommendations, the same hydration advice. But buried in a gastroenterology journal I found a reference to compounds that support gastric motility. Not laxatives. Not stool softeners. Things that help wake up the stomach itself.

One compound kept appearing in the research: celery seed extract.

Not celery juice cleanses. Not the wellness influencer stuff. The actual extract, studied for its ability to support digestive enzyme production and keep the stomach moving. It doesn't force anything. It supports the natural contractions your medication is suppressing.

That was the dam. Not removing it — the medication needs to stay — but opening a channel through it so the river doesn't dry up completely.

But motility was only part of it.

The sulfur burps — the ones that had humiliated me in that meeting — those happen because food sits in your stomach so long that bacteria start breaking it down before your digestive system can. The gas has nowhere to go but up. I needed something that neutralized that gas at the source.

I found the answer two weeks later. Chlorophyll. Not the trendy water drops. The actual compound, which binds to gases produced by bacterial fermentation in a stalled stomach and neutralizes them before they become those rotten-egg eruptions.

Two pieces now. Something to help the dam let water through. Something to neutralize the gas building up behind it.

But I kept thinking about downstream. Even if my stomach started moving food again, my intestines had been running dry for months. They needed support to handle what was finally coming through.

That's when I found prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber that had made my bloating worse — that was like pushing more material through a jammed system. Prebiotic fiber feeds the bacteria in your lower gut that keep things moving once food actually reaches them. It supports the river downstream. But only if the river is actually flowing.

Three pieces. Motility at the top. Gas neutralization in the middle. Downstream support at the bottom. Each one alone wouldn't solve it. The whole system had to work together.

I spent nights searching for something that combined all three. Most of what I found was incomplete — a motility supplement here, a chlorophyll dropper there, a fiber powder that was the same bulk fiber I'd already tried.

Then I found Motilli.

Small company. Three ingredients. Celery seed extract for motility. Chlorophyll for gas. Prebiotic fiber for downstream flow. In a gummy — which mattered more than I expected, because swallowing capsules on a stomach that won't empty is its own kind of misery.

I almost didn't order it. I'd been burned too many times. But the formulation matched the research so precisely that I figured I'd rather waste money on something that made sense than keep spending on Miralax that didn't.

The first week, nothing dramatic happened. A little less pressure after meals. The bloating went from a seven to maybe a five. I told myself it was probably placebo.

Day nine, I had a normal bowel movement. Not a Miralax-forced event. Not forty-five minutes of straining. A normal, unremarkable trip to the bathroom that I almost didn't register because it happened the way it's supposed to happen.

I sat there afterward and cried. I'm a grown woman who cried on her toilet because her body worked the way it's supposed to work. That's what the sentence does to you. It makes normal feel like a miracle.

By week three, the sulfur burps were gone. I sat through an entire staff meeting without calculating an exit strategy.

By the end of the first month, I'd stopped taking Miralax entirely. The Dulcolax in my purse expired and I threw it away.

My husband noticed before I said anything. Not the bathroom — he noticed I was eating dinner again. Staying at the table instead of retreating to the couch after four bites.

"You seem like yourself," he said one night.

My prescriber asked what I'd changed at my next appointment. She wrote down the name.

My sister-in-law — the one who'd whispered at Easter — started Zepbound two months later. I handed her a bottle and said "take two every morning. Give it six weeks." She texted me at week three: "The burps are gone and I went to the bathroom like a normal person."

I've been on Mounjaro for eleven months now. Forty-one pounds gone. And I am no longer serving the sentence.

For five months I believed there were only two options: stay on the medication and suffer, or quit and gain it all back. I thought the sentence was the price of the weight loss.

It wasn't. The suffering was misdirected treatment. Five months of pouring water at the bottom of a dry riverbed when the dam was at the top the entire time.

Your GLP-1 slows your stomach. Everything downstream suffers. And every remedy in your medicine cabinet right now was built for a digestive system that's working normally — not one that's been deliberately slowed down by a medication.

You don't have to serve the sentence. You just have to stop treating the wrong end of the river.
creative.title: Every laxative I tried was aimed at the wrong end of my body
